entries.title: Harry Houdini Died 100 Years Ago This Halloween: Was He Really Killed by a Punch to the Stomach?
entries.summary: This Halloween marks the 100th anniversary of the death of famed escape artist Harry Houdini. Today, most of us know more about the manner of that death than we do about any of the feats of escape artistry that made him famous in the first place. As the story goes, he’d mastered his own body […]
entries.content:
This Hal­loween marks the 100th anniver­sary of the death of famed escape artist Har­ry Hou­di­ni. Today, most of us know more about the man­ner of that death than we do about any of the feats of escape artistry that made him famous in the first place. As the sto­ry goes, he’d mas­tered his own body to the extent that he could tight­en his abdom­i­nal mus­cles so as to with­stand even the hard­est punch to the gut. Or at least that’s the image he let cir­cu­late: tak­ing it as a chal­lenge, a stu­dent and ama­teur box­er turned up and offered his fist to Hou­di­ni as an unex­pect­ed test. A week and a half lat­er, the great escapol­o­gist was dead of peri­toni­tis.

It seemed that the blow he sus­tained had rup­tured Hou­dini’s already-inflamed appen­dix, and that remained the wide­ly accept­ed, if not med­ical­ly air­tight, expla­na­tion for near­ly a cen­tu­ry. Yet there was always some­thing too dra­mat­i­cal­ly neat in the tale of a man famed for defy­ing death being done in by noth­ing more than a thought­less young man’s suck­er punch. Gen­er­a­tions of enthu­si­asts have offered expla­na­tions of their own, some more plau­si­ble than oth­ers, but few inves­ti­ga­tions into this qua­si-leg­endary demise have been con­duct­ed as seri­ous­ly as the one under­tak­en in our time by retired urol­o­gist Lar­ri­an Gille­spie, author of Hou­di­ni: The Man Who Died Twice.

When she had the chance to exam­ine his death cer­tifi­cate, Gille­spie noticed appar­ent irreg­u­lar­i­ties that led her down the rab­bit hole to “a paper trail of mis­state­ments and actions by more than a dozen peo­ple close to Hou­di­ni, includ­ing rel­a­tives and employ­ees,” writes the New York Times’ Robin Pogre­bin, “includ­ing a con­spir­a­cy to change his offi­cial death date to Octo­ber 31st, fix­ing his mem­o­ry to Hal­loween.” Accord­ing to her recon­struc­tion of events, Hou­di­ni actu­al­ly died the day before: not of appen­dici­tis, and not as a result of the young man’s punch. “Rather, she argues, the cul­prit was a bow­el obstruc­tion, brought on by a fibrous mass of chop suey that Hou­di­ni ate on Oct. 28.”

Emer­gency surgery took place the next day, but it was too late. “Sep­tic shock set in, Houdini’s fever spiked to 105 and his rapid breath­ing led to mus­cle spasms and uncon­scious­ness.” He was oper­at­ed on again the day after, and “Gillespie’s research into the death cer­tifi­cates indi­cates that the magi­cian died that after­noon at 1:26 p.m.” Gille­spie argues that the lack of a prop­er autop­sy helped con­ceal pos­si­ble med­ical mal­prac­tice and allowed Hou­dini’s wid­ow to col­lect a dou­ble-indem­ni­ty pay­ment for what was treat­ed as an acci­den­tal death. Even if accept­ed, her the­o­ry prob­a­bly won’t erase the cul­tur­al link between Hou­di­ni and Hal­loween. But the the­o­ry does add a new dimen­sion of irony to his life sto­ry: the man who could sur­vive a Chi­nese water tor­ture cell proved to be no match for Amer­i­can Chi­nese food.

entries.title: Hear an Hour of the Jazzy Background Music from the Original 1967 Spider-Man Cartoon
entries.summary: Ray Ellis had a six-decade career as a producer, arranger, and jazz composer. And while he’s best known for arranging music for Billie Holiday’s Lady in Satin (1958), he also enjoyed a long career orchestrating music for television. Working under a pseudonym “Yvette Blais” (his wife’s name), Ellis composed background music for the cartoon studio Filmation between 1968 and 1982. And, during […]
entries.content:
Ray Ellis had a six-decade career as a pro­duc­er, arranger, and jazz com­pos­er. And while he’s best known for arrang­ing music for Bil­lie Hol­i­day’s Lady in Satin (1958), he also enjoyed a long career orches­trat­ing music for tele­vi­sion. Work­ing under a pseu­do­nym “Yvette Blais” (his wife’s name), Ellis com­posed back­ground music for the car­toon stu­dio Fil­ma­tion between 1968 and 1982. And, dur­ing the late 60s, he notably cre­at­ed the back­ground and inci­den­tal music for the orig­i­nal Spi­der-Man car­toons.

Above, hear Ray Ellis’ Spi­der-Man sound­track. The show’s talk­ing parts and sound effects have been removed as much as pos­si­ble, then “pieced back togeth­er into com­plete form,” by a YouTu­ber who uses the moniker “11db11.” All of the music from Sea­son 1 is includ­ed, plus many record­ings from Sea­sons 2 and 3. It’s worth not­ing that the 52 episodes from the orig­i­nal 1967 Spi­der-Man TV series have been com­plete­ly restored. You can pur­chase them on DVD online.

Note: An ear­li­er ver­sion of this post appeared on our site in 2017.

entries.title: Watch Rome Rise, Fall, and Rise Again in a Three-Minute 3D Timelapse
entries.summary: Scholars disagree on when, exactly, Rome fell. But if you watch the new video from City 3D Timelapse above, you’ll understand the lack of debate on the question of whether it fell. Around the turn of the sixth century AD, buildings start vanishing at a rate that soon turns alarming; long before the end of […]
entries.content:
Schol­ars dis­agree on when, exact­ly, Rome fell. But if you watch the new video from City 3D Time­lapse above, you’ll under­stand the lack of debate on the ques­tion of whether it fell. Around the turn of the sixth cen­tu­ry AD, build­ings start van­ish­ing at a rate that soon turns alarm­ing; long before the end of the first mil­len­ni­um, it’s clear that Rome has been plunged into very hard times indeed. In the video’s accel­er­at­ed visu­al his­to­ry, that much-scru­ti­nized 500-year span pass­es in a lit­tle more than five sec­onds. Just one minute lat­er, it has spread not just beyond the old city lim­its, but beyond the very frame of the aer­i­al view, becom­ing the vast urban­ized region we know today.

Leg­end has it that Rome was found­ed in 753 BC, when Romu­lus killed his twin broth­er Remus. As reflect­ed by the video, archae­o­log­i­cal evi­dence sug­gests that the area was set­tled ear­li­er, though the tra­di­tion­al date of Rome’s found­ing rough­ly coin­cides with the emer­gence of what we know as the Roman King­dom.

There fol­low the Roman Repub­lic, the Roman Empire, the medieval era — when the once-for­mi­da­ble Eter­nal City was left prac­ti­cal­ly for dead  — the Renais­sance, the Roman Baroque peri­od, the indus­tri­al era, and final­ly, our time of glob­al­iza­tion. For ref­er­ence, the clas­si­cal archae­ol­o­gist Gio­van­ni Pirane­si went to Rome and drew his influ­en­tial etch­ings of its ruins around the 1:55 mark of this three-minute video.

Not that the Rome cap­tured in Pirane­si’s Vedute bears much resem­blance to the Rome of the twen­ty-first cen­tu­ry, for bet­ter or for worse. You can still see the Colos­se­um by moon­light, but the ambi­ence won’t be the same: the over­growth has long since been scraped off, and the car­go shorts are out in force year-round. Regard­less, no city is best appre­ci­at­ed through its land­marks alone, not even the mod­ern Rome so long both cel­e­brat­ed and dis­missed as an open-air muse­um. Watch­ing it rise, fall, and rise again from above with­in the length of a Euro­vi­sion song reminds us that it was­n’t built, or rebuilt, in a day — and that, in the face of often-for­mi­da­ble dif­fi­cul­ties, it even now man­ages to put up some­thing new once in a while.

entries.title: Christopher Lee Reads Edgar Allan Poe: “The Raven,” “The Fall of the House of Usher,” “The Murders in the Rue Morgue” & More
entries.summary: Sir Christopher Lee and Edgar Allan Poe went way back. Or at least they went as far back as 1969, the year of The Oblong Box, a loose and lurid film adaptation of the eponymous story starring Lee and the also Poe-associated Vincent Price. Lee plays the doctor to whom a gang of grave-robbers delivers […]
entries.content:
Sir Christo­pher Lee and Edgar Allan Poe went way back. Or at least they went as far back as 1969, the year of The Oblong Box, a loose and lurid film adap­ta­tion of the epony­mous sto­ry star­ring Lee and the also Poe-asso­ci­at­ed Vin­cent Price. Lee plays the doc­tor to whom a gang of grave-rob­bers deliv­ers Price’s char­ac­ter, an Eng­lish­man dis­fig­ured in a voodoo cer­e­mo­ny who fakes his own death in order to escape the cap­tiv­i­ty of his broth­er. What­ev­er its enter­tain­ment val­ue, the pic­ture does­n’t rank espe­cial­ly high in the canon of Poe adap­ta­tions. Nor, for that mat­ter, does the orig­i­nal sto­ry rank along­side works like “The Pit and the Pen­du­lum,” “The Fall of the House of Ush­er,” “The Cask of Amon­til­la­do,” or “The Black Cat.”

You can hear Lee him­self read all those macabre, imag­i­na­tive sto­ries and oth­ers besides in the YouTube playlist above. Some of the record­ings come from Christo­pher Lee Reads Edgar Allan Poe Tales of Hor­ror, the 1979 bud­get-label cas­sette pre­vi­ous­ly fea­tured here on Open Cul­ture. Oth­ers include Lee’s per­for­mances of “The Masque of the Red Death,” “The Tell-Tale Heart,” “Hop-Frog,” and “The Mur­ders in the Rue Morgue,” which is com­mon­ly cred­it­ed with launch­ing the entire genre of detec­tive fic­tion.

Though now most wide­ly remem­bered as a hor­ror actor, the pro­lif­ic Lee proved com­mand­ing in a vari­ety of gen­res: in the final decade of his life, he appeared in numer­ous crime pic­tures, adap­ta­tions of The Gold­en Com­pass and Char­lie and the Choco­late Fac­to­ry, and sev­er­al Star Wars and Lord of the Rings movies.

Not that he’d left Poe behind. Among the last cred­its Lee racked up in his life­time is Extra­or­di­nary Tales, from 2013, a five-sto­ry anthol­o­gy film in which he nar­rates “The Fall of the House of Ush­er.” Though British, his dis­tinc­tive man­ner and slight­ly mid-Atlantic accent were as ver­sa­tile on the screen as they were in read­ings of Poe, whose writ­ing dates from a time when more than a few Amer­i­cans still con­sid­ered lit­er­a­ture itself an import from across the pond. This Hal­loween, if you don’t have the hours free for a com­plete lis­ten-through of the playlist do con­sid­er at least putting on “The Raven.” It remains a mat­ter of debate among Poe enthu­si­asts to what extent Lee’s deliv­ery of “nev­er­more” real­ly cap­tures the spir­it of the poem, but it would be hard to imag­ine a more appro­pri­ate fig­ure to pre­side over All Hal­lows’ Eve.

entries.title: What Ancient Latin Sounded Like, And How We Know It
entries.summary: Latin is a language As dead as dead can be; It killed the Romans long ago, And now it’s killing me. That famed ditty isn’t likely to resonate with many modern school children, but interest in ancient Rome remains fairly robust. We’ve come to accept that those stately ruins were once covered in graffiti. We […]
entries.content:
Latin is a lan­guage

As dead as dead can be;

It killed the Romans long ago,

And now it’s killing me.

That famed dit­ty isn’t like­ly to res­onate with many mod­ern school chil­dren, but inter­est in ancient Rome remains fair­ly robust.

We’ve come to accept that those state­ly ruins were once cov­ered in graf­fi­ti.

We can recre­ate their meals from hors d’oeuvres (Boiled Eggs with Pine Nut Sauce) to dessert (Pear Pati­na).

Ther­mae Romae, a pop­u­lar Japan­ese man­ga-cum-fea­ture-film, took us inside Emper­or Hadri­an’s bath­house.

But what did the Romans sound like?

Kirk Dou­glas’ Spar­ta­cus? Or Lau­rence Olivier’s Cras­sus?

The HBO series Rome upheld the tra­di­tion of British accents.

Ani­ma­tor Josh Rud­der of NativLang did a fair amount of dig­ging in ser­vice of find­ing out What Latin Sound­ed Like, above.

(And he seems to have done so with­out the help of Derek Jarman’s NSFW Sebas­tiane, the only fea­ture film to be filmed entire­ly in ser­mo vul­garis or vul­gar Latin.)

Instead, he draws from ancient rhetori­cian Quin­til­ian and Virgil’s poet­ic meter. Scroll back­ward through the Romance lan­guages, and you’ll see Ger­man­ic tribes trad­ing with and fight­ing ancient Roman troops.

The result is not so much a recon­struc­tive pro­nun­ci­a­tion guide as a lin­guis­tic detec­tive sto­ry.

Note: An ear­li­er ver­sion of this post appeared on our site in 2016.

entries.title: In 1897, London’s Lampposts Dispensed Hot Coffee, Tea, and “Fluid Beef”
entries.summary: Any reader of Victorian literature will wonder how much a ha’penny was actually worth in those days. For a little more than a year at the very end of that period, it could buy you a cup of coffee, cocoa, milk, tea, or “fluid beef” — which would pour out of a lamppost on the […]
entries.content:
Any read­er of Vic­to­ri­an lit­er­a­ture will won­der how much a ha’pen­ny was actu­al­ly worth in those days. For a lit­tle more than a year at the very end of that peri­od, it could buy you a cup of cof­fee, cocoa, milk, tea, or “flu­id beef” — which would pour out of a lamp­post on the cor­ner. The Plu­to Lamp, as it was brand­ed, made its debut at the Vic­to­ri­an Era Exhi­bi­tion, which was held in 1897 to cel­e­brate the Queen’s Dia­mond Jubilee. Amid such attrac­tions as a 360-degree panora­ma of ancient Rome, Pep­per’s ghost illu­sions, and over 1,200 works of art by the likes of J. M. W. Turn­er, John Con­sta­ble, and 180 spe­cial­ly select­ed female artists, a bev­er­age-dis­pens­ing street­light might seem mun­dane. Yet apart from being a tech­no­log­i­cal mar­vel in its own way, it also pre­saged the tech­nol­o­gy-sat­u­rat­ed streets one day to come.

Not long after the Vic­to­ri­an Era Exhi­bi­tion, Plu­to Lamps appeared in sev­er­al Lon­don loca­tions, includ­ing Exmouth Street in Clerken­well, Leices­ter Square, and Rose­bery Avenue. In addi­tion to the illu­mi­na­tion of their sur­round­ings, and the drinks warmed by the excess heat thus gen­er­at­ed, they in some cas­es offered post­cards and four-to-the-pen­ny cig­a­rettes for sale as well.

How­ev­er much atten­tion the Plu­to Lamps attract­ed as a nov­el­ty, this was still the infan­cy of the mod­ern vend­ing machine, whose defi­cien­cies had yet to be ful­ly worked out. It proved impos­si­ble, at the time, to defeat the enter­pris­ing scoundrels who used round pieces of tin in place of gen­uine cur­ren­cy, and in any case, main­te­nance costs seem to have proven unex­pect­ed­ly high. (To say noth­ing of the prospect of drink­ing out of an enam­el cup on a chain, shared with the entire pub­lic, which sure­ly put off even some Vic­to­ri­ans.)

All of the Plu­to Lamps were decom­mis­sioned before the end of the nine­teenth cen­tu­ry, but they’d done their bit to expand pub­lic ideas of what was pos­si­ble in the urban pub­lic realm. “For over a cen­tu­ry, lamp posts would again do lit­tle more than shine light on to the city streets below,” writes Lukas Neck­er­mann in Smart Cities, Smart Mobil­i­ty. “But by the ear­ly twen­ty-first cen­tu­ry, the spir­it of the Plu­to Lamps returned. City infra­struc­ture and street fur­ni­ture would once again become mul­ti-pur­pose, mul­ti-use, entre­pre­neur­ial, and con­nect­ed.” And indeed, though talk of “smart cities” may now sound as dat­ed and unap­peal­ing as that of flu­id beef, lamp­posts have more recent­ly been giv­en such side jobs as vehi­cle charg­ing, envi­ron­men­tal pro­tec­tion, and even crime pre­ven­tion. That last brings back to mind the Clerken­well Plu­to Lamp, equipped as it was with a tele­graph recorder con­nect­ed straight to Scot­land Yard: a device that, had it last­ed longer, might have inspired many a Vic­to­ri­an nov­el­ist.

entries.title: Sears Sold 75,000 DIY Mail Order Homes Between 1908 and 1939, and Transformed American Life
entries.summary: Two of the books that most shaped American culture both happened to bear the nickname “The Big Book.” While the second of these, the A.A. Manual, published in 1939, changed the country with 12-Step recovery groups, the first of these, the Sears Catalog, transformed America with mass consumption, offering customers in every part of the […]
entries.content:
Two of the books that most shaped Amer­i­can cul­ture both hap­pened to bear the nick­name “The Big Book.” While the sec­ond of these, the A.A. Man­u­al, pub­lished in 1939, changed the coun­try with 12-Step recov­ery groups, the first of these, the Sears Cat­a­log, trans­formed Amer­i­ca with mass con­sump­tion, offer­ing cus­tomers in every part of the coun­try access to mod­ern con­ve­niences and retail goods of all kinds at unheard of prices. Begin­ning in 1908, Sears start­ed sell­ing entire hous­es, in approx­i­mate­ly 25-ton kits trans­port­ed by rail­road, con­sist­ing of 30,000 pre-cut parts, plumb­ing and elec­tri­cal fix­tures, and up to 750 pounds of nails.

“In an era before com­mer­cial avi­a­tion and long-haul truck­ing,” Curbed mar­vels, “Sears, Roe­buck & Co. set up an oper­a­tion that would pack­age and ship more than 400 dif­fer­ent types of homes and build­ings to any­body who had the cash and access to a cat­a­log.”

They start­ed small, and just as they didn’t come up with the con­cept of the mail order cat­a­log, Sears didn’t invent the kit house, though they sug­gest as much in their telling of the sto­ry. Instead they may have tak­en the idea from anoth­er com­pa­ny called Aladdin. Aladdin hous­es have been for­got­ten, how­ev­er, and even Sears’ main com­peti­tor, Mont­gomery Ward, didn’t catch up until 1921 and only last­ed ten years in the kit house busi­ness.

Sears hous­es, on the oth­er hand, are cel­e­brat­ed and sought out as mod­els of the ear­ly 20th cen­tu­ry Amer­i­can home, and for good rea­son. Between 1908 and 1939, Sears sold 70–75,000 hous­es in 447 dif­fer­ent styles all over the coun­try. “From Crafts­man to Cape Cods, they offered a cus­tom home at bud­gets and sizes that could accom­mo­date any size fam­i­ly,” writes Pop­u­lar Mechan­ics.

These Sears homes weren’t cheap low-end hous­es. Many of them were built using the finest qual­i­ty build­ing mate­ri­als avail­able dur­ing that time. It’s not uncom­mon to find Sears homes today with oak floors, cypress sid­ing, and cedar shin­gles.

What’s even more extra­or­di­nary is that 50% of these were built by the home­own­ers them­selves, usu­al­ly, as in a barn-rais­ing, with the gen­er­ous help of fam­i­ly, friends, and neigh­bors. The oth­er half sold were built pro­fes­sion­al­ly. “Often,” writes Messy Nessy, “local builders and car­pen­try com­pa­nies pur­chased homes from Sears to build as mod­el homes and mar­ket their ser­vices to poten­tial cus­tomers.”

These hous­es could have a sig­nif­i­cant effect on the char­ac­ter of a neigh­bor­hood. Not only could poten­tial buy­ers see first­hand, and par­tic­i­pate in, the con­struc­tion. They could also order the same or a sim­i­lar mod­el, cus­tomize it, and even—as the com­pa­ny tells us in its own short his­to­ry of the “Sears Mod­ern Home”—design their own homes and “sub­mit the blue­prints to Sears, which would then ship off the appro­pri­ate pre­cut and fit­ted mate­ri­als.”

Sears sounds mod­est about its impact. The com­pa­ny writes it was not “an inno­v­a­tive home design­er” but instead “a very able fol­low­er of pop­u­lar home designs but with the added advan­tage of mod­i­fy­ing hous­es and hard­ware accord­ing to buy­er tastes.” Yet Sears hous­es aren’t beloved for their for­ward-look­ing designs, but for their stur­di­ness and vari­ety, as well as for their impact on “the emo­tion­al lives of rur­al folk,” as Messy Nessy puts it.

“The Sears mail-order cat­a­logues were sit­ting on kitchen coun­ter­tops inside mil­lions of Amer­i­can homes, allow­ing poten­tial home­own­ers to both visu­al­ize their new home and pur­chase it as eas­i­ly as they might have bought a new toast­er.” Build­ing a house required a lit­tle more invest­ment than plug­ging in a toast­er, and required a 75-page instruc­tion book, but that’s anoth­er part of why Sears house hunters are such a ded­i­cat­ed bunch, awestruck at each still-stand­ing mod­el they’re able to pho­to­graph and match up with its cat­a­log illus­tra­tions and floor plans.

In its first year of pro­duc­tion, 1908, Sears sold only one mod­el, num­ber 125, an Eight-Room Bun­ga­low Style House for $945, adver­tised as “the finest cot­tage ever con­struct­ed at a price less than $1500.” In 1918, the com­pa­ny moved from a num­ber­ing sys­tem to named mod­els, most of which sound like the names of cozy small towns and bed­room com­mu­ni­ties: Ade­line, Bel­mont, Maple­wood, Aval­on, Kil­bourne, Del Ray, Stone Ridge…. (See a full list of these mod­els at The Arts & Crafts Soci­ety web­site.)

In the years Sears sold hous­es, between 54 and 44 per­cent of Amer­i­cans lived in rur­al areas, and these con­sti­tut­ed Sears’ most loy­al cus­tomers, giv­en that the cat­a­log allowed them to pur­chase things they could buy nowhere else, includ­ing ten room colo­nial man­sions like The Mag­no­lia, avail­able from 1913 to 1922 for $6,488, or rough­ly $88,000—a steal if you can put in the work. This was the largest and most expen­sive mod­el the com­pa­ny offered, “a three-sto­ry, eight room neo-Geor­gian with a two-sto­ry columned por­ti­co, porte-cochere, and sleep­ing porch­es.” (Mint juleps and ser­vants’ quar­ters not includ­ed.)

Sears even­tu­al­ly offered three build qual­i­ties, Hon­or Bilt, Stan­dard Built, and Sim­plex Sec­tion­al. At the low­est end of the price and build spec­trum, the com­pa­ny notes, “Sim­plex hous­es were fre­quent­ly only a cou­ple of rooms and were ide­al for sum­mer cot­tages.” Many of its low-end and ear­ly mod­els did not include bath­rooms, and the com­pa­ny sold out­hous­es sep­a­rate­ly. But due to inno­v­a­tive con­struc­tion meth­ods, even the least expen­sive hous­es held up well.

Because the com­pa­ny lost most of the records after its kit house busi­ness fold­ed, it can be dif­fi­cult to iden­ti­fy a Sears house. And because even the “youngest of Sears homes,” Pop­u­lar Mechan­ics points out, is now going on nine decades old, they all require a sig­nif­i­cant amount of care.” The blog Kit House Hunters has found over 18,000 Sears hous­es still stand­ing across the coun­try, most of them in the North­east and Mid­west, where they sold best. (One com­mu­ni­ty in Elgin, IL has over 200 ver­i­fied Sears homes.)

In the video at the top, you can see a few of those well-built Sears hous­es still lived in today. The short How to Archi­tect video above points out that “Sears had a mas­sive impact on the busi­ness of home-build­ing, and… the busi­ness of pre-fab­ri­ca­tion, is alive and well today.” For a look at the vari­ety and intri­ca­cy of the Sears Mod­ern Home designs, see this Flickr gallery with over 80 images of cat­a­log pages, illus­trat­ed homes, and floor plans. And if you think you might be liv­ing in one of these hous­es, many of which have been grant­ed his­toric sta­tus, find out with this handy 9‑step guide for iden­ti­fy­ing a Sears Kit Home.

Note: An ear­li­er ver­sion of this post appeared on our site in 2018.

Relat­ed Con­tent

When Frank Lloyd Wright Designed a Dog­house, His Small­est Archi­tec­tur­al Cre­ation (1956)

entries.title: Doctor Who’s Tom Baker Plays Douglas Adams’ Digital “Agent” in the AI-Predicting Hyperland (1990)
entries.summary: Cast your mind, if you will, back to the year 2020. It now feels like a different time, what with the spreading COVID-19 pandemic and the heated sociopolitical battles being waged online, and indeed in the (socially distanced) streets. That spring, we featured here on Open Culture an amusing retro-technological diversion called Hyperland. First broadcast on BBC2, […]
entries.content:
Cast your mind, if you will, back to the year 2020. It now feels like a dif­fer­ent time, what with the spread­ing COVID-19 pan­dem­ic and the heat­ed sociopo­lit­i­cal bat­tles being waged online, and indeed in the (social­ly dis­tanced) streets. That spring, we fea­tured here on Open Cul­ture an amus­ing retro-tech­no­log­i­cal diver­sion called Hyper­land. First broad­cast on BBC2, the pro­gram stars The Hitch­hik­er’s Guide to the Galaxy author Dou­glas Adams as him­self and Doc­tor Who’s Tom Bak­er as his agent. “You want fif­teen per­cent?” the for­mer asks the lat­ter when they first meet in a vast waste­land of flick­er­ing tele­vi­sion sets. Not at all: “I’m here to do your every slight­est bid­ding,” Bak­er explains, “to fetch and car­ry for you, to work tire­less­ly and self­less­ly on your behalf, always ready, always will­ing, no job too small or too menial.”

Today, we can hard­ly share in Adams’ bewil­der­ment, famil­iar as we are with the notion of what Bak­er calls a “soft­ware agent,” an “arti­fi­cial and com­plete­ly cus­tomiz­able per­son­al­i­ty” with “instant access to every piece of infor­ma­tion stored dig­i­tal­ly any­where in the world: any pic­ture or film, any sound, any book, any sta­tis­tic, any fact, any con­nec­tion between any­thing you care to think of.” We must remind our­selves that Hyper­land was pro­duced in 1990, when these lines would have struck all but the most com­put­er-savvy and for­ward-look­ing view­ers as sheer sci­ence fic­tion. Even three decades there­after, they still sound­ed more or less like an ele­vat­ed ver­sion of ordi­nary late-twen­ti­eth-cen­tu­ry tech­no-opti­mism. Here in 2026, Bak­er’s ser­vices are close to being con­sid­ered a basic neces­si­ty, at least in Sil­i­con Val­ley and its glob­al provinces.

Not so very long ago, Hyper­land looked star­tling­ly pre­scient about the rise of the World Wide Web, which would soon let its users seek out their own desired pieces of infor­ma­tion and media, active­ly mov­ing through links between them, in a man­ner unlike the pas­sive view­ing expe­ri­ence of tele­vi­sion (with which it would, as no one then knew, one day con­verge). This was an unfa­mil­iar idea to most peo­ple in 1990; hence the vari­ety of clear and enter­tain­ing ways in which the pro­gram breaks down its tech­no­log­i­cal basis, pulling up clips from its onscreen “data­base” like an inter­view with Ted Nel­son, who coined the term hyper­text. Like mul­ti­me­dia, that word may car­ry a whiff of antiq­ui­ty today, but it was once on the lips of prac­ti­cal­ly every tech­nol­o­gist in pop­u­lar cul­ture — in a man­ner rem­i­nis­cent of the lex­i­con that has sprung from new devel­op­ments in arti­fi­cial intel­li­gence over the past few years.

At times, Bak­er’s char­ac­ter now looks almost real­is­tic, as when Adams asks him to knock off the obse­quious­ness, or when he pulls up Kurt Von­negut’s the­o­ry of sto­ry form before Adams ful­ly gets the ques­tion out. Yet Hyper­land devotes lit­tle time to AI per se. The pro­gram appeared in the wake of the eight­ies’ AI boom, when “expert sys­tems” promised to solve prob­lems in indus­try, med­i­cine, and oth­er sec­tors, but many of the field­’s larg­er ambi­tions went unre­al­ized. There fol­lowed a long “AI win­ter” in research and devel­op­ment, in whose cli­mate Baker-as-“agent” would have been a means of human­iz­ing an abstract-seem­ing con­cept of orga­niz­ing and nav­i­gat­ing infor­ma­tion. Not that all his enthu­si­as­ti­cal­ly prof­fered ser­vices draw unqual­i­fied enthu­si­asm from Adams, who pos­sessed a rare com­bi­na­tion of Cal­i­forn­ian technophil­ia and British skep­ti­cism. His fas­ci­na­tion with human­i­ty’s dig­i­tal future is ours — and so is his wari­ness.

entries.title: Hear How Clare Torry’s Vocals on Pink Floyd’s “The Great Gig in the Sky” Made the Song Go from Pretty Good to Downright Great
entries.summary: Smack in the middle of Pink Floyd’s classic Dark Side of the Moon sits a song many listeners may hear as an extended bridge between the two true centerpieces, “Time” and “Money.” But I’ve always thought of “The Great Gig in the Sky” as the album’s true center, a swirling, swinging, soulful prog-rock masterpiece, carried to […]
entries.content:
Smack in the mid­dle of Pink Floy­d’s clas­sic Dark Side of the Moon sits a song many lis­ten­ers may hear as an extend­ed bridge between the two true cen­ter­pieces, “Time” and “Mon­ey.” But I’ve always thought of “The Great Gig in the Sky” as the album’s true cen­ter, a swirling, swing­ing, soul­ful prog-rock mas­ter­piece, car­ried to stratos­pher­ic heights by British singer Clare Tor­ry. The song’s word­less gospel vocal makes it an ecsta­t­ic, even hope­ful, tent pole sup­port­ing Dark Side’s bril­liant­ly cyn­i­cal songs about the banal­i­ty and injus­tice of mod­ern life.

“The Great Gig in the Sky,” that is to say, pro­vides much-need­ed emo­tion­al release in an album that can sound, writes Alex­is Petridis, “like one long sigh.” Yet if you know the sto­ry of Dark Side of the Moon and of Clare Torry’s defin­ing con­tri­bu­tion, you’ll know that her incred­i­ble soar­ing vocal was sheer hap­pen­stance, an impro­vi­sa­tion by a young singer brought in at the last minute by pro­duc­er Alan Parsons—and one who wasn’t a par­tic­u­lar fan of the band. (“If it had been The Kinks,” she remem­bered, “I’d have been over the moon.”)

Tor­ry reluc­tant­ly stepped into the stu­dio and asked the band, “Well, what do you want?” Basi­cal­ly, she says, “they had no idea.” An iso­lat­ed track from Alan Par­sons’ 1973 mix (above) strips the song down to piano, drums, slide gui­tar, and Torry’s voice. Ear­ly live ver­sions of the song in 1972 had fea­tured Bible read­ings and record­ed speech­es by con­ser­v­a­tive writer Mal­colm Mug­geridge; in the final ver­sion, these gave way to snip­pets of the band’s crew and friends answer­ing ques­tions about death.

When Tor­ry went into the vocal booth and put on the head­phones, she would have heard an even more stripped-down mix. Giv­en no oth­er instruc­tion than “we don’t want any words,” she decid­ed, “I have to pre­tend to be an instru­ment.”

Torry’s vocal is so dis­tinc­tive that she even­tu­al­ly won a set­tle­ment in 2005 for a co-song­writ­ing cred­it with Wright—an out­come some song­writ­ing experts agree was ful­ly jus­ti­fied since she essen­tial­ly cre­at­ed a new melody for the song. In the inter­view above, hear Tor­ry describe how she “had a lit­tle go” and, after some guid­ance from David Gilmour and a can of Heineken, casu­al­ly knocked out one of the most thrilling vocal per­for­mances in rock his­to­ry.

Note: An ear­li­er ver­sion of this post appeared on our site in 2017.
